definition: The number of particles visibly alive at once from one emitter is approximately its Rate (particles per second) multiplied by its Lifetime (seconds each particle persists) — so a HIGH rate is not automatically a performance or visual-clutter problem if Lifetime is correspondingly LOW, and the two properties should be judged together, never rate alone.
purpose: Judge and control how visually busy (and how expensive) an emitter is by reasoning about the product of two properties together, rather than reacting to either one in isolation.
visible_effect: The same apparent density of particles on screen can be produced by many different rate/lifetime pairs with the same product; conversely, a high rate paired with a high lifetime produces a visibly cluttered, "spammed" result even if neither value looks extreme alone.
psychological_or_gameplay_effect: Too many simultaneous particles from one emitter reads as noisy/low-quality ("it looks bad, but it's also just too many particles"); the same visual richness achieved with fewer concurrent particles (low lifetime, higher rate) reads as controlled.
physical_interpretation: A direct queueing-theory identity (arrival rate × dwell time = concurrent count) applied to particle emission, not a Roblox-specific rule.
use_cases: judging whether an emitter is "spammy" before changing any one property blindly
deliberately trading rate against lifetime to keep a target concurrent-particle count while changing how fast individual particles appear to move through their lifecycle
non_use_cases: reading Rate alone as a performance signal — a high rate with a very short lifetime can have a low concurrent count, and this formula is exactly why that is not a contradiction
interactions: phase_offset_dual_emitter_for_persistent_glow (this same video) — that technique deliberately doubles concurrent count for one specific glow in exchange for removing a visible pulse, a cost this same formula makes legible

Cadence's `EFFECT_ROLES` budget shares (VFX-011, `ai/vfxspec.js`) cap `maxParticles` per role (primary 100%, supporting 50%, residual 25%) — a role's budget cap is exactly the ceiling this video's rate×lifetime product should be checked against
cadence_representation: `VFXSPEC_FIELDS.budget` (`{maxParticles}`) already caps a compiled effect's particle count, scaled by its declared `role`'s share — but VFXSpec does not expose Rate and Lifetime as independently authored fields the way Roblox's ParticleEmitter does (both are subsumed into the chosen `primitive`/`scale`), so a caller cannot directly reason "rate × lifetime" against `maxParticles` the way this video's presenter does by eye. The video's mental model (two dials whose PRODUCT matters) is one level more granular than VFXSpec's declarative surface exposes.
control_surface: `compile_effect`'s `budget.maxParticles`, capped by the `role`'s `EFFECT_ROLES` share; nothing exposes rate/lifetime individually for a caller to multiply and check against that cap.
detection_and_measurement_methods: `pnx_profile`/`vfx_performance_report` measure a compiled effect's actual particle/performance cost at runtime — the closest existing analogue to eyeballing rate×lifetime, though measured after the fact rather than computed from the two authored dials directly.
generation_or_modification_methods: `compile_effect`'s `budget`/`scale` fields adjust the ceiling and overall size/rate together; there is no direct per-field rate or lifetime control to multiply against it.
failure_modes: reacting to a high Rate value by lowering it, when a shorter Lifetime would have solved the same clutter problem while keeping particles appearing more frequently
judging clutter from a single emitter's rate alone rather than its concurrent count, missing a genuinely spammy low-rate-but-long-lifetime emitter
roblox_considerations: Rate and Lifetime are both plain ParticleEmitter properties; this is Roblox-specific only in which two named properties multiply this way, not in the underlying arithmetic.
performance_implications: Direct: concurrent particle count is the actual rendering cost driver, and this formula is how to estimate it from the two authored dials without needing to run the effect and count.
examples: "You can have a high rate, but still have a low lifetime and it won't really spam as much... it's just less particles at once, which is good" (video @ 39:19–39:31)

"if I put this down like six, it doesn't look all that much worse. And it's just less particles at once" (video @ 39:43–39:50, lowering Rate specifically because the accompanying Lifetime was already short)

the presenter deliberately over-cranking a specs emitter's rate to demonstrate the bad case directly: "I don't want to take something like this, like the specs, and crank it up. ... it looks bad, but it's also just too many particles" (video @ 40:09–40:21)
evidence_status: video: https://youtu.be/u2o-wHKDlpw @ 39:19–40:21 — Twist reasons explicitly about rate against lifetime as a joint budget while auditing his own finished effect for particle spam; experimental until validated
